result: The Aurora B kinase, as part of the chromosome passenger complex (CPC), is essential for mitotic regulation and has been identified as a cancer chemotherapy target.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by citations to established prior research (Carmena et al., 2012; Vader et al., 2006; Kelly and Funabiki, 2009; Krenn and Musacchio, 2015; Meraldi et al., 2004; Portella et al., 2011; Jing and Chen, 2021). These claims provide background context from the literature.

result: The [Aurora B/IN-box] complex is activated by autophosphorylation at two sites (Aurora B Thr248 and IN-box TSS motif), increasing activity by at least 100-fold. Prior structural understanding was limited to partially phosphorylated states, with no crystal structure available for the unphosphorylated complex.
evaluation: Claims C5-C10 are supported by citations to prior research (Zaytsev et al., 2016; Bishop and Schumacher, 2002; Honda et al., 2003; Sessa et al., 2005; Sessa and Villa, 2014; Elkins et al., 2012; Abdul Azeez et al., 2019). These claims establish the knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

result: Protein dynamics play critical roles in enzyme catalysis, including in protein kinases, but the effect of phosphorylation on [Aurora B/IN-box] dynamics was previously unknown.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15 are supported by citations to prior research on protein dynamics and kinase regulation (Boehr et al., 2006; Tzeng and Kalodimos, 2012; Xie et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2015; Ahuja et al., 2019; Pegram et al., 2021; Taylor and Kornev, 2011; Foda et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019; Cyphers et al., 2017; Dodson and Bayliss, 2012; Gilburt et al., 2017; Pitsawong et al., 2018; Ruff et al., 2018; Tomlinson et al., 2022). These establish the rationale for studying dynamics.

result: HDX-MS reveals that the unphosphorylated [Aurora B/IN-box]no-P is structurally disordered in multiple regions (including αC-helix, catalytic loop, activation segment, αG-helix, and IN-box), while the fully phosphorylated [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P is more rigid and structurally organized. The complex remains intact under HDX conditions.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C22-C27, C33-C35, C37-C38, C46-C49 are supported by HDX-MS data presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures, and mass photometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4. The HDX measurements were performed in triplicate with appropriate controls, and the interpretation that higher deuterium uptake indicates greater flexibility is standard in the field. The mass photometry confirms complex integrity at the experimental concentration.

result: The αC-helix and other regions showing HDX differences are known to play critical roles in kinase function based on prior research.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32, C36, C40 are supported by citations to prior research (Kornev and Taylor, 2015; Kornev et al., 2008; Leroux and Biondi, 2020; Bayliss et al., 2003; Ahuja et al., 2019; Arrington and Robertson, 2000; Chitta et al., 2009; Ferraro et al., 2004; Sperry et al., 2012; Walters et al., 2013). These provide context for interpreting the HDX results.

result: The IN-box805-825 region exhibits EX1 kinetics in both phosphorylation states, indicating reversible folding/unfolding, with more frequent unfolding in the unphosphorylated state.
evaluation: Claims C39, C41-C45 are supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The observation of two isotopic envelopes is a hallmark of EX1 kinetics, and the interpretation that the higher mass peak appearing more rapidly indicates more frequent unfolding is consistent with established HDX theory (C40).

result: MD simulations (2.8 μs) show that in [Aurora B/IN-box]no-P, the C-terminal IN-box remains unstructured, while in [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P, phosphorylation rapidly stabilizes a defined conformation where IN-boxArg847 interacts with Aurora BpThr248, with additional stabilization by three Aurora B arginines. The simulation structure differs from the [Aurora C/IN-box]all-P crystal structure in the C-terminal IN-box region.
evaluation: Claims C50-C62 are supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures. The simulations were stable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and the structural differences between phosphorylation states are clearly documented. The comparison with the Aurora C crystal structure is appropriate. However, the 2.8 μs simulation time may be insufficient to fully sample conformational space, which the authors acknowledge in the Discussion.

result: The authors suggest that the [Aurora C/IN-box]all-P crystal structure represents the final active state, while their [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P simulation likely captures an intermediate state, due to the high dynamics and entropic nature of the IN-box C-terminus.
evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C135-C137 are speculative (labeled as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While the reasoning is plausible based on the MD data and comparison with Aurora C, these are interpretations rather than direct observations. The authors acknowledge simulation time limitations and the entropic nature of the IN-box, but definitive proof would require additional experimental validation or longer simulations.

result: MD simulations show that the dynamics of Aurora B and IN-box are coupled: the N-terminal IN-box (IN-box807-837) and adjacent Aurora B regions (αC-helix, ATP-binding site) exhibit higher RMSF in [Aurora B/IN-box]no-P than in [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P, suggesting that disorder spreads between partners in the unphosphorylated state.
evaluation: Claims C65-C72 are supported by RMSF analysis from MD simulations shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2. The RMSF data clearly show higher fluctuations in the unphosphorylated state, and the interpretation that dynamics are coupled is reasonable given the proximity of these regions. The inference that IN-box acts as a negative regulator in the unphosphorylated state (C71) is a logical conclusion from the data.

result: Phospho-mimetic mutations (Thr→Glu or Ser→Glu) and phospho-null mutations in the activation loop resulted in catalytically dead enzymes, necessitating an alternative approach.
evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are based on experimental observations (evidence_type: DATA). While the manuscript does not show the data for these failed mutants, this is a reasonable negative result that motivated the protein ligation approach. The observation is consistent with the known limitations of phospho-mimetic mutations.

result: A synthetic peptide ligation approach was used to generate partially phosphorylated intermediates ([Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P and [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P), with a single IN-boxPhe845Cys mutation as a 'scar'. Both semisynthetic constructs showed similar activity to wt [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P after ATP-Mg incubation.
evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by methodology description and enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A. The protein ligation approach is well-established (Ghosh et al., 2011), and the validation that the semisynthetic constructs achieve full activity confirms that the mutation and ligation process do not fundamentally alter enzyme function.

result: Partially phosphorylated intermediates show low activity: [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P exhibits ~10% and [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P ~5% of maximum initial rate. The sum (~15%) is much less than the fully phosphorylated enzyme, demonstrating synergistic rather than independent effects of the two phosphorylation sites.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 3C. The measurements were performed with appropriate controls and replicates. The calculation showing that the sum of individual activities (15%) is much less than the full activity (100%) provides strong evidence for synergy. This is a key finding of the paper.

result: Kinetic analysis of [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P shows vmax is ~3-fold lower and KM is 10-fold higher than [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P, resulting in 20-fold lower catalytic efficiency. This suggests that IN-box phosphorylation strongly affects substrate binding and moderately affects catalysis.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B. The Michaelis-Menten analysis is appropriate, and the interpretation that the large KM increase indicates a substrate binding defect is standard enzymology. The data quality appears good with error bars shown.

result: HDX-MS of partially phosphorylated intermediates shows intermediate levels of protection. Each phosphorylation alone causes partial structuring of the entire complex, but full structural stability requires both phosphorylations. Specific regions show differential protection: IN-boxαA in [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P and Aurora BαG in [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P.
evaluation: Claims C87-C95 are supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures. The measurements were performed with appropriate controls (including the Phe845Cys mutation control). The observation that each phosphorylation causes ~50% of the full protection in key catalytic regions (C89) is particularly compelling evidence for the synergistic model. The HDX data on the TAA mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) confirms that αG rigidification is independent of IN-box phosphorylation.

result: MD simulations of [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P show that the phosphorylated TSS motif is stabilized by adjacent positively charged residues and interacts with the N-lobe of Aurora B, but does not extend to the C-lobe.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Video 3. The simulations show a clear difference in IN-box conformation compared to [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P, providing a structural explanation for why IN-box phosphorylation alone is insufficient for full activity.

result: MD simulations of [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P show that the C-terminal IN-box is rapidly attracted to Aurora BpThr248, with IN-boxArg843 forming a stable electrostatic interaction after 0.25 μs. The final structure resembles [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5 and Video 4. The rapid formation of the IN-boxArg843-Aurora BpThr248 interaction is clearly documented in Figure 5C. This provides a structural explanation for why activation loop phosphorylation can partially organize the IN-box even without TSS phosphorylation.

result: Autoactivation kinetics show that all three unphosphorylated or partially phosphorylated complexes can achieve full activity, but with different rates: [Aurora B/IN-box]no-P is slowest, [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P is much faster than [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A. The experiments were performed with appropriate controls and replicates (standard deviations shown). The different autoactivation rates provide key information about the mechanism.

result: Kinetic analysis identifies Aurora B activation loop phosphorylation as the slow, intramolecular (cis) step and IN-box TSS phosphorylation as the fast, intermolecular (trans) step in autoactivation.
evaluation: Claims C106-C110 are supported by kinetic test data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The Dodson kinetic test (concentration-dependence analysis) is an established method for distinguishing cis vs. trans reactions. The overlapping normalized traces for [Aurora B/IN-box]IN-P indicate concentration-independent (cis) phosphorylation, while the concentration-dependent traces for [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P indicate trans phosphorylation. This is a key mechanistic finding.

result: Mutagenesis shows that IN-boxArg847Ala reduces catalytic efficiency 4-fold (mainly via 5-fold increase in KM), identifying this residue as important for substrate binding. IN-boxArg843Ala reduces efficiency 2.5-fold without affecting KM, suggesting a role in catalysis.
evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Table 1. The mutagenesis experiments provide functional validation of the MD simulation predictions about the roles of these arginine residues. The differential effects on KM vs. kcat support distinct roles in substrate binding vs. catalysis.

result: PCA of MD simulations shows that the type of movement in PC1 depends on phosphorylation state. Only [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P shows organized vibrational deformation (cosine content 0.01) that coordinates opening/closing and activation loop movement, while other states show random deformations (cosine content 0.5-0.9).
evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by PCA analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 6A and Video 5. The cosine content analysis is an established method for distinguishing organized motions from random diffusion (Hess, 2000). The low cosine content for [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P PC1 provides strong evidence for coordinated motion in the fully phosphorylated state.

result: PCA analysis shows that [Aurora B/IN-box]no-P explores a wide conformational space, [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P is more restricted, and [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P is forced into three well-defined regions corresponding to coordinated oscillations. Only full phosphorylation achieves coordinated movement of lobes and activation loop for efficient catalysis.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C. The progressive restriction of conformational space with increasing phosphorylation is clearly visible in the plots. This provides a dynamic explanation for the synergistic activation mechanism.

result: Structuring after phosphorylation is a general activation mechanism for protein kinases, and the [Aurora C/IN-box] crystal structure showed that the phosphorylated IN-box stabilizes a compact, active conformation.
evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by citations to prior research (Hsu et al., 2008; Steichen et al., 2010; Abdul Azeez et al., 2019). These provide context for interpreting the current findings.

result: The N-terminal IN-box exhibits EX1-like HDX kinetics suggesting reversible folding/unfolding, but remains associated with Aurora B (confirmed by mass photometry). The higher unfolding rate in the unphosphorylated state transfers disorder to Aurora B, supporting the conclusion that unphosphorylated IN-box acts as a negative regulator.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 are supported by HDX-MS data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), mass photometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), and MD simulation data (Figure 2D and F). The integration of multiple lines of evidence strengthens the conclusion about the negative regulatory role of unphosphorylated IN-box.

result: Phosphorylation of the Aurora B activation loop leads to partial structuring and conformational changes, while full phosphorylation of both sites results in a structured, coordinated enzyme complex where the phosphorylated IN-box acts as a positive regulator.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are supported by integration of HDX-MS and MD simulation data shown throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figure 7. This represents the main conclusion of the paper, synthesizing all the experimental and computational findings.

result: The C-terminal IN-box is a highly entropic unit with fast diffusion dynamics controlled by phosphorylation state, showing highest disorder when unphosphorylated, partial organization in [Aurora B/IN-box]loop-P, and better organization in [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P.
evaluation: Claim C134 is supported by MD simulation data, particularly the Aurora C simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The RMSF analysis clearly shows the high flexibility of the C-terminal IN-box region and its phosphorylation-dependent organization.

result: The IN-box plays a major role in Aurora B structural conformations and subdomain motion synchronization. Global domain movement is proposed to be directly linked to the catalytic cycle and likely controls substrate binding and product release.
evaluation: Claim C138 is well-supported by the combined HDX-MS, MD, and PCA data. Claim C139 is more speculative (evidence_type includes SPECULATION) but is a reasonable inference based on the observation that only [Aurora B/IN-box]all-P exhibits synchronized motions and the established role of domain motions in other kinases.

result: The dynamic changes observed in the IN-box likely follow the same trend in full-length INCENP context. The N-terminal INCENP region is required for CPC localization and high local concentration, crucial for rapid intermolecular activation.
evaluation: Claim C140 is an inference based on prior research showing that the IN-box is sufficient for activation. Claim C141 is supported by citations to prior research (Wang et al., 2011a; Zaytsev et al., 2016). These claims address the relevance of the minimal system studied to the full-length protein in cells.

result: The autoactivation mechanism involves slow intramolecular Aurora B activation loop phosphorylation followed by rapid trans phosphorylation of IN-box TSS. The slow intramolecular step is obligatory only when the entire population is dephosphorylated.
evaluation: Claims C142-C143 are supported by the kinetic data (Figure 5D-E) and represent a refinement of the prior model (Zaytsev et al., 2016). The clarification that the slow cis step is only obligatory for a fully dephosphorylated population is an important mechanistic insight.

result: Phosphorylation gradients of Aurora B substrates exist in cells and play regulatory roles in mitosis. The low activity of partially phosphorylated intermediates (5-10%) and two-step autoactivation are consistent with the ability to form steep phosphorylation gradients.
evaluation: Claims C144-C147 are supported by citations to prior research (Fuller et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011a; Afonso et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2013; Uehara et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; Zaytsev et al., 2016). Claim C148 is an inference connecting the current findings to the gradient phenomenon, which is reasonable but would benefit from additional modeling or experimental validation.

result: Unlike Aurora A, which can be activated independently by TPX2 binding or activation loop phosphorylation in different cellular contexts, Aurora B follows a single synergistic activation pathway requiring coincident phosphorylation of both the activation loop and the IN-box TSS motif.
evaluation: Claims C149-C152 are supported by citations to prior research on Aurora A (Dodson and Bayliss, 2012; Kufer et al., 2002; Levinson, 2018; Joukov et al., 2010). Claim C153 is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript. This comparison highlights the unique regulatory mechanism of Aurora B.

result: The Aurora B/IN-box interface represents a potential target for developing Aurora B-specific drugs that would disrupt allosteric activation.
evaluation: Claim C154 is speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION, INFERENCE) and represents a suggestion for future drug development. While the findings do identify the Aurora B/IN-box interface as functionally important, demonstrating its suitability as a drug target would require additional medicinal chemistry and pharmacological studies.
